newsitem.title: USA: Bob Dole made major gambles but lost.
newsitem.headline: Bob Dole made major gambles but lost.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
At the age of 73, Bob Dole proved himself to a be a man willing to take big gambles to capture the White House, and he lost.
His biggest roll of the dice was to resign last May as Senate Majority leader, a job he loved, to prove he was serious about beating Bill Clinton.
"I will seek the presidency with nothing to fall back on but the judgment of the people and nowhere to go but the White House or home," he said in a tearful speech.
His defeat by Clinton on Tuesday means he must now go into unwanted retirement after one of the most remarkable careers in post-war American politics.
Dole travelled a classic journey from poverty in the Great Depression, through European battlefields to the corridors of power. He called becoming president "the last mission of my generation."
But the 73-year-old Kansan failed in that mission, running far behind Clinton -- a 50-year-old from a "baby-boom" generation very different from his.

A plain-speaking man from the plains of Kansas, Dole found himself fighting uphill against an incumbent president helped by a favourable economy, a flare for campaigning and an ability to communicate in the television age that he lacked.
Dole's campaign came under attack from friend and foe alike as he lurched from issue to issue hoping to find one that would catch fire.
It was only in the last days of the campaign that he began to score points with the public over Clinton's acceptance of millions of dollars from foreign interests and foreign-born businessmen.
But by then it was too late.
Many people criticised Dole for not giving a clear reason for wanting to be president and even when he gave his best explanation it backfired.

In his acceptance speech at the Republican convention in August, Dole declared, "Let me be a bridge to an America that only the unknowing call a myth, let me be a bridge to a time of tranquility, faith and confidence in action. To those who say it was never so, that America has not been better, I say, you're wrong, and I know because I was there. I have seen it. I remember."
Clinton cleverly seized on the speech and turned it around, declaring that he wanted to "build a bridge to the 21st century" in what became the central slogan of his campaign.

Over and again, Dole proved willing to take risks in his White House quest. In August, he turned his back on long dedication to budget-balancing and proposed a 15 percent tax- cut package. But many voters were unconvinced and said they believed it would blow a hole in the budget deficit he had pledged to cut.
The man who as a child in Kansas knew neighbours who committed suicide because of debt, became a convert to the idea that economic growth should come first and debt would take care of itself.
He did win praise for his bold choice of bitter rival Jack Kemp -- a tax-cut champion -- as his running mate. That gave his campaign a short-lived jolt of energy and momentum.
But as the campaign wore on and little seemed to work, Dole became increasingly strident, attacking Clinton for his ethical standards on a range of issues.

He began his third run for the White House in April 1995, 50 years to the week after he was wounded as a U.S. Army second lieutenant in Italy. He led an assault on a German machinegun nest and a shell destroyed his right shoulder, paralysed his right arm, broke vertebrae, riddled his body with shrapnel and robbed him of a kidney.

Twice decorated for heroism, he spent 39 months in hospitals before returning to civilian life. He went to law school, unable to write and getting through with the help of his first wife, who transcribed lecture notes for him.

He lost the key New Hampshire primary in February to conservative firebrand Pat Buchanan, but kept his cool and relied on his superior organisation, money and the support of the Republican establishment. Buchanan and other rivals -- who attacked Dole savagely and may have done him permanent damage for the fight with Clinton -- were driven from the field.

Robert Joseph Dole was born on July 22, 1923, one of four children of a grain elevator manager in Russell, Kansas. After the war he became a lawyer and joined politics. He won a House of Representatives seat in 1960 and a Senate seat in 1968.
Twice serving as Senate Majority Leader, he was an effective middle-of-the-road legislator, well-liked among Democrats as well as Republicans.
Dole twice sought the Republican nomination without success in 1980 and 1988, and was then-President Gerald Ford's vice presidential running mate in 1976.

After divorce from his first wife, in 1975 he married Elizabeth Hanford, who has been a federal trade commissioner and transportation and labour secretary in Republican Cabinets and is now on leave as president of the American Red Cross. He has one daughter, Robin, from his first marriage.
